title: Labor market cooling continues into the second quarter
text:
Payroll growth slowed for a third consecutive month, with the establishment survey showing an addition of just under ninety thousand jobs, well below the twelve-month average. The deceleration was broadest in goods-producing sectors, where manufacturing employment contracted outright for the first time since the prior downturn. Services hiring held up better but showed clear signs of moderation, particularly in professional and business services, where temporary help placements fell for a fifth straight month, a series that has historically led broader payroll turns by one to two quarters.

The unemployment rate ticked up two tenths to just above four percent, driven mostly by a rise in labor force participation rather than outright job losses, a distinction that matters for how policymakers read the print. Average hourly earnings growth cooled to the slowest pace in three years, easing concerns about a wage-price spiral even as headline inflation remains above target. Job openings continued their gradual descent from the extraordinary highs of the post-pandemic period, and the ratio of openings to unemployed workers is now back near its pre-pandemic norm.

Taken together, the data support the view that the labor market is normalizing rather than breaking down, though the pace of deceleration bears close watching heading into the back half of the year. A further slowing in hiring, absent an offsetting pickup in productivity, would begin to weigh on aggregate income growth and, with a lag, consumer spending.
